posts.body_html:
Mike, your answer is sort of what I expected. We've seen leucos growing in dry, compact sand, but know that when there are heavy rains the whole field floods and then slowly drains.
Did you get an ID on the snake? There are some really nice color forms of rat snakes up around the gulf coastal areas that encompass the Florida panhandle, Alabama, and Mississippi. We've also seen some large Black Racers up there. They are lightning fast and diurnal hunters, so make for a startling discovery when you come across one.
Sonia, the snake bites to worry about in pitcher plant country are Cottonmouths and rattlesnakes (3 species). Coral snakes are around, but they are shy.

posts.body_html: As Kiwiearl said, your field experience is absolutely priceless,sunbelle, and is greatly appreciated! I have no idea what species of snake it was, but by your description, it could have very well been a black racer. Due to my ignorance towards snakes, I steer clear of all of them just in case. I did encounter a copperhead once in Alabama, and they are very hard to spot because they blend in with the environment quite well. Good rule of thumb: don't mess with them, and they won't mess with you. In any case, they're really beautiful-check out those patterns!

posts.body_html:
That really is good camo.

We have no idea down here! No snakes, only one poisonous spider that's secretive and reluctant to bite, no scorpions, no large mammalian predators. In fact the only mammalian predators are the one's we humans have introduced and they are small to tiny, in the case of stoats, ferrets, weasels, rats, Australian Possums and hedgehogs, or pets/livestock in the case of cats, dogs and pigs. None of these when feral are any real danger to humans where they occur.

Our wild places are "nothing to fear but fear itself" places. You can happily walk around in our bush all day long in bare feet. We're literally not conditioned to even be on the look out for anything despite our hard wiring.

Of course, the worst predator of all is, as usual, the humans....

posts.body_html:
Thank you Dory! Sorry for replying almost a year later...haven't seen this thread since. The good news is, I have more photos to share!!!



A super-white plant:



Even the plain jane clones here were outstanding:




Notice the hood flopping over a bit: this is likely due to slight dehydration (the soil here was very dry). In California, our humidity is very low, and if I let the soil dry out like that, the traps would be crispy after a day. Here in the wild, the humidity is so high, the traps don't fry, they wilt first. Regardless of the water stress, check out how much white is on this trap!



Same trap zoomed out a bit:



A freshly opened trap, GOSH!!!



Same trap, there's almost 4" (10cm) of white pigments on this thing!



Okay, Axel was on this trip, and he ruined maybe 1 or 2 of my 1000's of photos. Damon, on the other hand, is in a lot of them. Everyone has their own talent, haha! Yes, that's Damon in the background, to the right...nevermind the white leucophylla:



Can you see the preying mantis on this trap? I blew up the picture a bit so everyone can get a closer look:



A standard, good looking plant:


Lynx spider, as common as crabs in leuco territory:






Var albas were quite abundant here:



Strange how some traps have red coloration in them, but there were a lot of wherryi/leuco. back-crosses here, so I wouldn't be surprised if this had rubra wherryi mixed in it. Back-cross a S. x readii enough times and it's hard to tell that rubra was ever mixed in:


More photos to come!

posts.body_html:
some more photos!


Damon caught a butterfly! Strange how butterflies are near impossible to photograph, but when they land on your hand (presumably, they're going for sweat), they stay there and aren't easily spooked away:



Baby Preying mantis:





Slight bronze or reddish color:




A white beauty!


Same plant:



Standard bright white clone, this trap seems to have just opened:



No matter what bog or what state we were in, S. leucophylla had barely caught anything this time of year. An Exyra moth, probably laying eggs to eat up this trap later on:


No matter how "plain" these traps looked, they were still really beautiful:








Here we go! I think this is one that's wilting as described in a previous comment. Not the best example because we can't see the other trap on the same plant, but I probably have better examples of this at another site (that's for another post):



Not sure if the lid is wilting, or just back-crossed with alata:






Check out all the activity in the background:





Too bad this one didn't open yet:





Lots of great genetics here:






It was pretty dry this time of year:



Love the amount of white on these traps:






out of this world-the netting and white contrast is spectacular:




Rival to hurricane creek white, notice the spider legs:



As you can see, blinding white plants are an exception to the rule, it's not like the entire population is nothing but white plants. Same goes for the hurricane creek white site before it was destroyed: bright white plants existed, but they were a minority:


Here, var. albas were a minority, but with a high frequency:




Still have more photos to come!
